ety.text: From вз- (vz-) + -бира́ть (-birátʹ) + -ся (-sja), with meaning following the corresponding perfective взобра́ться (vzobrátʹsja).

Inherited from Old East Slavic въздымати (vŭzdymati). Usually explained from Proto-Slavic *vъzdymati (“blow up”), from *dymati, iterative of *dǫti. Alternatively, although less likely, it might be a result of rebracketing of подыма́ть (podymátʹ) as по-дыма́ть, at least in the modern sense.

Traditionally explained as borrowing from Old Church Slavonic въз- (vŭz-); compare inherited cognate вз- (vz-). However, there is an opinion about independent development, compare the words взойти (vzojti), взобраться (vzobratʹsja), взорвать (vzorvatʹ), which indicate the presence of a second /ъ/ in the prefix, which makes it possible to create a strong position for /ъ/ and transition to /o/. Also compare възогъловие (*възъголовие) in birch bark manuscript №469. Per Zaliznyak, prefix възъ- arose by analogy with the Old East Slavic prefixes like отъ- and подъ-.

x: У́лица, зали́тая со́лнечным све́том, пестре́ла я́ркими пя́тнами кумачо́вых руба́х и весёлым оска́лом бе́лых зубо́в, грызу́щих подсо́лнухи; игра́ли вразбро́д гармо́ники, стуча́ли чугу́нные пли́ты о костя́шки, и голоси́сто ора́л пету́х, вызыва́я на бой сосе́дского петуха́.

ety.text: Borrowed probably from French hystérique, from Latin hysterica passiō, from Ancient Greek ὑστέρα (hustéra), feminine of ὕστερος (hústeros), from Proto-Indo-European *udero-.

Possessive of кала́шник (kalášnik), i.e. literally, “belonging to (son of) the 'kalach-man'”, where кала́ч (kaláč) is the Russian word for a specific type of twisted white bread. From кола́ч (koláč) (through akanye), from Proto-Slavic *kolačь, a derivation of *kolo (“circle, wheel”). Cognate to Ukrainian and Bulgarian кола́ч (koláč), Serbo-Croatian kòlač, Slovak and Czech koláč, Polish kołacz.

ety.text: Literally, “highbush cranberry”. Attested early 20th century. Derives from a 19th century joke about a French teller of tall tales who claims to have rested in the shade of a cranberry plant during a supposed visit to Russia; in reality, cranberries in the wild are tiny dwarf plants. Nabokov pointed out that the expression literally translates to “highbush cranberry” (Viburnum opulus) in English, but in Russian (unlike English) it appears absurd because Russian uses entirely different terms for tall shrubs in the genus Viburnum (кали́на (kalína)) and dwarf plants in the subgenus Oxycoccus (кл…

ety.text: From Old East Slavic туча (tuča), from Proto-Slavic *tǫča, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tenk- (“to contract”). Compare the Slavic Old Church Slavonic тѫча (tǫča), Ukrainian ту́ча (túča), Polish tęcza and the Non-Slavic Gothic 𐌸𐌴𐌹𐍈𐍉𐌽 (þeiƕōn) and Old Norse þéttr. Unrelated to Russian ту́чный (túčnyj) (which is related to тук (tuk) and historically had nonnasal vowel у (u)).
